name: Roguelike
description: Short runs, procedural variety and builds that change every time, with progression between runs.

pillars.name: Every Run Is Different
pillars.feeling: I can't wait to see what this run gives me
pillars.rulesOut: runs that always play out the same

pillars.name: Death Teaches
pillars.feeling: losing makes me better next time
pillars.rulesOut: deaths that feel random or unfair

pillars.name: Builds That Break the Game
pillars.feeling: finding a combo that goes wild
pillars.rulesOut: items that are only small stat bumps

gameExamples.heading: Pitch
gameExamples.text: A top-down action roguelike where each descent stacks up a wild build of relics before the run inevitably ends.

gameExamples.heading: Core Loop
gameExamples.text:
1. Start a run.
2. Clear a room.
3. Pick a reward.
4. Descend, die eventually, and unlock something for next time.

docs.title: Runs
docs.summary: How a run is built and paced: rooms, encounters and rewards.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can start a fresh run any time.
- As a player, I can see how far I got.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - A run summary at the end.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- A run lasts 20-30 minutes.
- Runs always start in the same first room.

docs.title: Encounters
docs.summary: Fights, events and choices along the way.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can fight different enemy mixes each room.
- As a player, I can choose between risky and safe rooms.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Room icons that show what's behind each door.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text: - Every floor has one optional elite room.

docs.title: Rewards
docs.summary: What the player is offered during a run, and when.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text: - As a player, I can choose one reward from three after each room.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Reward choices with clear descriptions.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text: - Rarer rewards appear less often but never zero.

docs.title: Procedural Generation
docs.summary: Generating floors, rooms and layouts that stay fair.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Floors are built from hand-made room templates connected on a graph; rules ensure a path to the exit and a fair spread of rewards.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UFloorGenerator`: builds the room graph from a seed
- `URoomTemplate`: a hand-made room asset

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Room templates per floor.
- Generation rules in a data asset.

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Dark dungeon with saturated highlights so enemies and pickups pop.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text: - Modular dungeon packs designed for top-down cameras.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text: - Detailed floors that hide projectiles.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can attack, dodge and use abilities.
- As a player, I can fight many enemies at once.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Clear telegraphs on enemy attacks.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text: - Dodging makes the player briefly invulnerable.

docs.title: Combat Code
docs.summary: Attacks, damage, projectiles and status effects.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Attacks spawn hitboxes for a few frames; overlaps send damage events to anything with a health component. Status effects are applied as timed modifiers.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UCombatComponent`: starts attacks and spawns hitboxes
- `UHealthComponent`: takes damage, fires death events
- `UStatusEffect`: a timed modifier (burn, slow, stun)

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Attack data (damage, frames, hitbox size) in data assets.
- Status effects in a DataTable.

examples.heading: What to Avoid

docs.title: Builds
docs.summary: What makes each run play differently: items, upgrades and how they combine.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can combine items into a build.
- As a player, I can see what my build does.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - A build screen listing every item and its effect.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text: - No item is useless in every build.

docs.title: Synergies

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text: - As a player, I can discover items that work together.

examples.heading: The Player Sees

examples.heading: Rules

docs.title: Item Effects
docs.summary: How item effects are defined, stacked and applied.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Item effects are small objects that hook into gameplay events (on hit, on kill, on damage taken). Stacking rules decide how copies combine.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UItemEffect`: base class with event hooks
- `UBuildComponent`: the player's items and active effects

examples.heading: Data
examples.text: - Item definitions in data assets.

examples.text: Every item is recognizable from its icon alone.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text: - Icon packs with a consistent style and background.

docs.title: Meta Progression
docs.summary: Unlocks and progress that carry over between runs.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can unlock new options between runs or levels.
- As a player, I can see what I can unlock next.
- As a player, I can choose what to work toward.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- An unlock screen with locked and unlocked items.
- Progress bars toward the next unlock.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Unlocks add options, not raw power.
- Everything can be unlocked by playing.

docs.title: UI
docs.summary: Menus and HUD: what the player sees and can do outside the game world.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can start, pause and quit from clear menus.
- As a player, I can change graphics, audio and control settings.
- As a player, I can see the information I need during play without it covering the action.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A title screen, pause menu and settings screens.
- A HUD with only what matters right now.
- Button prompts that match my input device.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Every screen can be used with a gamepad as well as mouse and keyboard.
- Pausing stops gameplay time.
- Settings save immediately.

docs.title: UI Framework
docs.summary: How screens and widgets are built, opened, navigated and fed data.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Screens are UMG widgets pushed onto a stack by a UI manager subsystem. The top screen gets input; popping it returns to the one below. Gameplay talks to the HUD through events, never directly.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UProjectUISubsystem`: owns the screen stack and opens and closes screens
- `UScreenWidget`: base class for every full screen (menus, settings)
- `UHUDWidget`: the in-game HUD; listens to gameplay events

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Screen classes and their input modes in a data asset.
- Settings in the game user settings, saved per user.

docs.summary: Icons, fonts, panels and widget skins.

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Clean and readable first: flat shapes, high contrast, one accent color. Icons share one line weight and perspective.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- UI kits with matching icons, buttons and panels.
- Fonts licensed for games, with the character sets we localize to.
- Input prompt packs covering keyboard, Xbox and PlayStation.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Mixing icon packs with different styles.
- Ornate frames that crowd the screen.
- Fonts that are hard to read at small sizes.

docs.summary: Music, sound effects and ambience, and where each is used.

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Music sets the mood of each area; sound effects are short and punchy so they read over the music.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Music packs with loopable stems.
- Sound effect libraries with variations of each sound.
- Licenses that allow commercial use and streaming.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Tracks that don't loop cleanly.
- Effects with long tails that muddy fast moments.
- Mixing many libraries with different loudness.

docs.title: Save and Load
docs.summary: Meta progress, unlocks and run history.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: A save game object holds everything that persists. Systems register what they need saved; saving serializes it to a slot, loading restores it before the level starts. Saves carry a version number so old saves can be migrated.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `USaveSubsystem`: saves and loads slots, runs migrations
- `UProjectSaveGame`: the saved data, with a version field
- `ISaveable`: interface for systems that write and read their part

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Save slots in the platform's save location.
- A version number per save, bumped on every breaking change.
